title: When Should a Pay Raise Change Spending? — Modigliani & Friedman Permanent Income, Robert Hall’s (1978) Martingale Consumption Euler Equation & Campbell–Mankiw Rule-of-Thumb Income Sensitivity in BEA Data

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: If your boss announces a pay raise six months early, do you adjust spending when you hear the news or wait until the paycheck hits? Hall's (1978) permanent-income martingale says predictable income shouldn't jolt spending at payday—and Campbell & Mankiw measured how real households split that rule.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Stimulus checks, tax refunds, and interest-rate policy work completely differently depending on what fraction of households smooth life-cycle income vs. spend paycheck-to-paycheck.
keyTakeaways: Friedman and Modigliani argued rational forward-looking consumers smooth consumption across life-cycle permanent income.

Robert Hall (1978) proved a striking implication via the consumption Euler equation: only *unanticipated* news should move consumption, so lagged predictable income changes shouldn't predict consumption growth.

Campbell and Mankiw (1989) used instrumental variables on BEA aggregate data to estimate lambda ~ 0.5: roughly half of income goes to liquidity-constrained or rule-of-thumb consumers who spend when cash arrives.

vocab.meaning: First-order optimality condition equating today's marginal utility of consumption to discounted expected future marginal utility.
A sequence whose future change cannot be predicted from information already known today.
Empirical response of consumption growth to predictable income changes, violating pure frictionless permanent-income smoothing.

quiz.question: Under Robert Hall's (1978) pure rational-expectations permanent-income hypothesis, when should a pre-announced bonus change household consumption?
options: Only two years after it is deposited
When the news is first learned, with zero extra jump on the predictable payday itself
quiz.explanation: Forward-looking consumers without credit constraints incorporate expected income at announcement, leaving no predictable jump left on payday.
